Appendix A Photon-phonon mixing

As outlined in Sec. II.1, mixing between long-wavelength photon and phonon states needs to be taken into account when computing DM absorption rates in a polar crystal. Our starting point is the Lagrangian for an ionic lattice coupling to electromagnetism:

L=∑l​j(12​mj​𝒖˙l​j2−12​∑l′​j′𝒖l​j⋅𝐕l​j,l′​j′(2)⋅𝒖l′​j′+e​𝑬​(𝒙l​j0)⋅𝐙j∗⋅𝒖l​j)+∫d3​x​(−14​Fμ​ν​Fμ​ν+12​Aμ​Πμ​ν​Aν).L=\sum_{lj}\biggl(\frac{1}{2}\,m_{j}\dot{\boldsymbol{u}}_{lj}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\sum_{l^{\prime}j^{\prime}}\boldsymbol{u}_{lj}\cdot\mathbf{V}_{lj,l^{\prime}j^{\prime}}^{(2)}\cdot\boldsymbol{u}_{l^{\prime}j^{\prime}}+e\,\boldsymbol{E}(\boldsymbol{x}_{lj}^{0})\cdot\mathbf{Z}^{*}_{j}\cdot\boldsymbol{u}_{lj}\biggr)+\int d^{3}x\biggl(-\frac{1}{4}F^{\mu\nu}F_{\mu\nu}+\frac{1}{2}A_{\mu}\Pi^{\mu\nu}A_{\nu}\biggr). (41)

In the long wavelength limit, the leading electromagnetic coupling is via the electric dipole, as shown in the third term. Plugging in 𝑬=−∇A0−𝑨˙\boldsymbol{E}=-\nabla A_{0}-\dot{\boldsymbol{A}} and integrate by parts, we can write it in the familiar form of −∫d3xJμAμ=∫d3x(−ρA0+𝑱⋅𝑨)-\int d^{3}x\,J^{\mu}A_{\mu}=\int d^{3}x(-\rho A_{0}+\boldsymbol{J}\cdot\boldsymbol{A}), with

ρ(𝒙)=−e∑l​j(∇δ(3)(𝒙−𝒙l​j0))⋅𝐙j∗⋅𝒖l​j,𝑱(𝒙)=e∑l​j𝐙j∗⋅𝒖˙l​jδ(3)(𝒙−𝒙l​j0).\rho(\boldsymbol{x})=-e\sum_{lj}\bigl(\nabla\delta^{(3)}(\boldsymbol{x}-\boldsymbol{x}_{lj}^{0})\bigr)\cdot\mathbf{Z}^{*}_{j}\cdot\boldsymbol{u}_{lj}\,,\qquad\boldsymbol{J}(\boldsymbol{x})=e\sum_{lj}\mathbf{Z}^{*}_{j}\cdot\dot{\boldsymbol{u}}_{lj}\,\delta^{(3)}(\boldsymbol{x}-\boldsymbol{x}_{lj}^{0})\,. (42)

when expanded to linear order in 𝒖\boldsymbol{u}. The last term in Eq. (41) results from integrating out electron response. As explained in detail in Ref. [37], the photon self-energy Πμ​ν\Pi^{\mu\nu} can be related to the dielectric tensor of the medium, 𝜺\boldsymbol{\varepsilon} (taken to be the electronic contribution, usually denoted by 𝜺∞\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}_{\infty}, in the present case), and the photon Lagrangian can be written as

−14​Fμ​ν​Fμ​ν+12​Aμ​Πμ​ν​Aν\displaystyle-\frac{1}{4}F^{\mu\nu}F_{\mu\nu}+\frac{1}{2}A_{\mu}\Pi^{\mu\nu}A_{\nu} =12𝑨˙⋅𝜺⋅𝑨˙−12A0(∇⋅𝜺⋅∇)A0+A˙0(∇⋅𝜺⋅𝑨)−12(∂iAj)2+12(∇⋅𝑨)2.\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\dot{\boldsymbol{A}}\cdot\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}\cdot\dot{\boldsymbol{A}}-\frac{1}{2}A_{0}\left(\nabla\cdot\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}\cdot\nabla\right)A_{0}+\dot{A}_{0}(\nabla\cdot\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}\cdot\boldsymbol{A})-\frac{1}{2}\bigl(\partial_{i}A^{j}\bigr)^{2}+\frac{1}{2}(\nabla\cdot\boldsymbol{A})^{2}\,. (43)

It is convenient to choose a generalized Coulomb gauge, ∇⋅𝜺⋅𝑨=0\nabla\cdot\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}\cdot\boldsymbol{A}=0, and since the A0A_{0} field is non-dynamical, it can be immediately integrated out. We thus obtain

L\displaystyle L =\displaystyle= ∑l​j12​mj​𝒖˙l​j2−12​∑l​l′​j​j′𝒖l​j⋅𝐕l​l′​j​j′⋅𝒖l′​j′+e​𝑨​(𝒙l​j0)⋅𝐙j∗⋅𝒖˙l​j\displaystyle\sum_{lj}\frac{1}{2}\,m_{j}\dot{\boldsymbol{u}}_{lj}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\sum_{ll^{\prime}jj^{\prime}}\boldsymbol{u}_{lj}\cdot\mathbf{V}_{ll^{\prime}jj^{\prime}}\cdot\boldsymbol{u}_{l^{\prime}j^{\prime}}+e\,\boldsymbol{A}(\boldsymbol{x}_{lj}^{0})\cdot\mathbf{Z}^{*}_{j}\cdot\dot{\boldsymbol{u}}_{lj} (44)
+∫d3x[12𝑨˙⋅𝜺⋅𝑨˙−12(∂iAj)2+12(∇⋅𝑨)2+12ρ1∇⋅𝜺⋅∇ρ].\displaystyle+\int d^{3}x\biggl[\frac{1}{2}\dot{\boldsymbol{A}}\cdot\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}\cdot\dot{\boldsymbol{A}}-\frac{1}{2}\bigl(\partial_{i}A^{j}\bigr)^{2}+\frac{1}{2}(\nabla\cdot\boldsymbol{A})^{2}+\frac{1}{2}\,\rho\frac{1}{\nabla\cdot\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}\cdot\nabla}\rho\biggr].

To derive the Hamiltonian, we note the canonical momenta are:

𝒑l​j=∂L∂𝒖˙l​j=mj​𝒖˙l​j+e​𝑨​(𝒙l​j0)⋅𝐙j∗,𝑷⁡(𝒙)=∂ℒ∂𝑨˙​(𝒙)=𝜺⋅𝑨˙​(𝒙).\boldsymbol{p}_{lj}=\frac{\partial L}{\partial\dot{\boldsymbol{u}}_{lj}}=m_{j}\dot{\boldsymbol{u}}_{lj}+e\,\boldsymbol{A}(\boldsymbol{x}_{lj}^{0})\cdot\mathbf{Z}^{*}_{j}\,,\qquad\boldsymbol{P}(\boldsymbol{x})=\frac{\partial{\cal L}}{\partial\dot{\boldsymbol{A}}(\boldsymbol{x})}=\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}\cdot\dot{\boldsymbol{A}}(\boldsymbol{x})\,. (45)

Therefore,

H=∑l​j𝒑l​j⋅𝒖˙l​j+∫d3​x​𝑷⋅𝑨˙−L=Hph+HCoulomb+HEM+Hmix,H=\sum_{lj}\boldsymbol{p}_{lj}\cdot\dot{\boldsymbol{u}}_{lj}+\int d^{3}x\,\boldsymbol{P}\cdot\dot{\boldsymbol{A}}-L=H_{\text{ph}}+H_{\text{Coulomb}}+H_{\text{EM}}+H_{\text{mix}}\,, (46)

where

Hph\displaystyle H_{\text{ph}} =\displaystyle= ∑l​j𝒑l​j22​mj+12​∑l​l′​j​j′𝒖l​j⋅𝐕l​l′​j​j′⋅𝒖l′​j′,\displaystyle\sum_{lj}\frac{\boldsymbol{p}_{lj}^{2}}{2m_{j}}+\frac{1}{2}\sum_{ll^{\prime}jj^{\prime}}\boldsymbol{u}_{lj}\cdot\mathbf{V}_{ll^{\prime}jj^{\prime}}\cdot\boldsymbol{u}_{l^{\prime}j^{\prime}}\,, (47)
HCoulomb\displaystyle H_{\text{Coulomb}} =\displaystyle= −12∫d3xρ1∇⋅𝜺⋅∇ρ,\displaystyle-\frac{1}{2}\int d^{3}x\,\,\rho\,\frac{1}{\nabla\cdot\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}\cdot\nabla}\,\rho\,, (48)
HEM\displaystyle H_{\text{EM}} =\displaystyle= ∫d3​x​[𝑷⋅𝜺−1⋅𝑷+12​(∂iAj)2−12​(∇⋅𝑨)2+e22​∑l​j1mj​δ(3)​(𝒙−𝒙l​j0)​(𝑨⋅𝐙j∗)2],\displaystyle\int d^{3}x\,\biggl[\boldsymbol{P}\cdot\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}^{-1}\cdot\boldsymbol{P}+\frac{1}{2}\bigl(\partial_{i}A^{j}\bigr)^{2}-\frac{1}{2}(\nabla\cdot\boldsymbol{A})^{2}+\frac{e^{2}}{2}\sum_{lj}\frac{1}{m_{j}}\delta^{(3)}(\boldsymbol{x}-\boldsymbol{x}_{lj}^{0})\bigl(\boldsymbol{A}\cdot\mathbf{Z}^{*}_{j}\bigr)^{2}\biggr]\,,\quad (49)
Hmix\displaystyle H_{\text{mix}} =\displaystyle= −e∑l​j1mj𝑨(𝒙l​j0)⋅𝐙j∗⋅𝒑l​j.\displaystyle-e\sum_{lj}\frac{1}{m_{j}}\,\boldsymbol{A}(\boldsymbol{x}_{lj}^{0})\cdot\mathbf{Z}^{*}_{j}\cdot\boldsymbol{p}_{lj}\,. (50)

Note that while we have written 𝑨\boldsymbol{A} and 𝑷\boldsymbol{P} as 3-vectors, they are implicitly assumed to satisfy the gauge condition. This means that, in Eq. (49), 𝜺\boldsymbol{\varepsilon} should be projected onto the subspace satisfying the gauge condition before the inverse is taken.

We now consider the four terms in turn. First, as mentioned in Sec. II.1, we use the phonopy code with DFT calculations of the force constants 𝐕l​j,l′​j′(2)\mathbf{V}_{lj,l^{\prime}j^{\prime}}^{(2)} to diagonalize the lattice (phonon) Hamiltonian HphH_{\text{ph}}, giving

Hph=∑ν=13​n∑𝒌ων,𝒌​a^ν,𝒌†​a^ν,𝒌.H_{\text{ph}}=\sum_{\nu=1}^{3n}\sum_{\boldsymbol{k}}\omega_{\nu,\boldsymbol{k}}\hat{a}^{\dagger}_{\nu,\boldsymbol{k}}\hat{a}_{\nu,\boldsymbol{k}}\,. (51)

Second, the Coulomb term, HCoulombH_{\text{Coulomb}}, becomes more transparent when written as a momentum space integral:

HCoulomb=12​∫d3​k(2​π)3​|ρ~​(𝒌)|2𝒌⋅𝜺⋅𝒌,H_{\text{Coulomb}}=\frac{1}{2}\int\frac{d^{3}k}{(2\pi)^{3}}\frac{|\tilde{\rho}(\boldsymbol{k})|^{2}}{\boldsymbol{k}\cdot\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}\cdot\boldsymbol{k}}\,, (52)

with the charge density

ρ~(𝒌)=∫d3xe−i𝒌⋅𝒙ρ(𝒙)=−ie∑l​j𝒌⋅𝐙j∗⋅𝒖l​je−i𝒌⋅𝒙l​j0.\tilde{\rho}(\boldsymbol{k})=\int d^{3}x\,e^{-i\boldsymbol{k}\cdot\boldsymbol{x}}\rho(\boldsymbol{x})=-ie\sum_{lj}\boldsymbol{k}\cdot\mathbf{Z}^{*}_{j}\cdot\boldsymbol{u}_{lj}\,e^{-i\boldsymbol{k}\cdot\boldsymbol{x}_{lj}^{0}}\,. (53)

Expanding 𝒖l​j\boldsymbol{u}_{lj} in (a^ν,𝒌′+a^ν,−𝒌′†)(\hat{a}_{\nu,\boldsymbol{k}^{\prime}}+\hat{a}^{\dagger}_{\nu,-\boldsymbol{k}^{\prime}}) as in Eq. (11) and summing over ll picks out the 𝒌′=𝒌\boldsymbol{k}^{\prime}=\boldsymbol{k} modes. With the momentum integral discretized, ∫d3​k(2​π)3→1N​Ω∑𝒌\int\frac{d^{3}k}{(2\pi)^{3}}\to\frac{1}{N\Omega}\sum_{\boldsymbol{k}}, we find

HCoulomb=e24​Ω​∑ν,ν′,𝒌1ων′,𝒌​ων,𝒌​(𝒌⋅𝝃ν′,𝒌∗)​(𝒌⋅𝝃ν,𝒌)𝒌⋅𝜺⋅𝒌​(a^ν′,−𝒌+a^ν′,𝒌†)​(a^ν,𝒌+a^ν,−𝒌†),H_{\text{Coulomb}}=\frac{e^{2}}{4\Omega}\sum_{\nu,\nu^{\prime},\boldsymbol{k}}\frac{1}{\sqrt{\omega_{\nu^{\prime},\boldsymbol{k}}\omega_{\nu,\boldsymbol{k}}}}\frac{(\boldsymbol{k}\cdot\boldsymbol{\xi}^{*}_{\nu^{\prime},\boldsymbol{k}})(\boldsymbol{k}\cdot\boldsymbol{\xi}_{\nu,\boldsymbol{k}})}{\boldsymbol{k}\cdot\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}\cdot\boldsymbol{k}}\bigl(\hat{a}_{\nu^{\prime},-\boldsymbol{k}}+\hat{a}^{\dagger}_{\nu^{\prime},\boldsymbol{k}}\bigr)\bigl(\hat{a}_{\nu,\boldsymbol{k}}+\hat{a}^{\dagger}_{\nu,-\boldsymbol{k}}\bigr)\,, (54)

where

𝝃ν,𝒌≡∑j1mj​𝐙j∗⋅ϵν,𝒌,j.\boldsymbol{\xi}_{\nu,\boldsymbol{k}}\equiv\sum_{j}\frac{1}{\sqrt{m_{j}}}\,\mathbf{Z}^{*}_{j}\cdot\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{\nu,\boldsymbol{k},j}\,. (55)

As a technical note, while there is an option in phonopy (non-analytic correction) to also include HCoulombH_{\text{Coulomb}} in the diagonalization calculation, it seems to work only at k≳ωk\gtrsim\omega. Therefore, in our calculation, we use phonopy to diagonalize only HphH_{\text{ph}}, and include HCoulombH_{\text{Coulomb}} separately.

Next, we also write the photon Hamiltonian HEMH_{\text{EM}} in momentum space:

HEM=∫d3​k(2​π)3​[12​𝑷~​(𝒌)∗⋅𝜺−1⋅𝑷~​(𝒌)+12​𝑨~​(𝒌)∗⋅𝐊𝟐⋅𝑨~​(𝒌)],H_{\text{EM}}=\int\frac{d^{3}k}{(2\pi)^{3}}\biggl[\frac{1}{2}\boldsymbol{\tilde{P}}(\boldsymbol{k})^{*}\cdot\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}^{-1}\cdot\boldsymbol{\tilde{P}}(\boldsymbol{k})+\frac{1}{2}\,\boldsymbol{\tilde{A}}(\boldsymbol{k})^{*}\cdot\mathbf{K^{2}}\cdot\boldsymbol{\tilde{A}}(\boldsymbol{k})\biggr]\,, (56)

where

𝐊𝟐=k2​𝟙+e2Ω​∑j𝐙j∗​𝐙j∗Tmj−𝒌​𝒌.\mathbf{K^{2}}=k^{2}\mathbb{1}+\frac{e^{2}}{\Omega}\sum_{j}\frac{\mathbf{Z}^{*}_{j}\mathbf{Z}^{*T}_{j}}{m_{j}}-\boldsymbol{k}\boldsymbol{k}\,. (57)

We decompose the photon field 𝑨~\boldsymbol{\tilde{A}} into two orthogonal linear polarizations 𝒆1,𝒌⟂𝒆2,𝒌\boldsymbol{e}_{1,\boldsymbol{k}}\perp\boldsymbol{e}_{2,\boldsymbol{k}} which satisfy the gauge condition, 𝒌⋅𝜺⋅𝒆λ,𝒌=0\boldsymbol{k}\cdot\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}\cdot\boldsymbol{e}_{\lambda,\boldsymbol{k}}=0 (λ=1,2\lambda=1,2). We choose the basis in which the projection of 𝜺\boldsymbol{\varepsilon} onto the two-dimensional subspace, 𝒆λ′⋅𝜺⋅𝒆λ\boldsymbol{e}_{\lambda^{\prime}}\cdot\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}\cdot\boldsymbol{e}_{\lambda}, is diagonal, with eigenvalues ε1\varepsilon_{1}, ε2\varepsilon_{2}. Denote the projection of 𝐊𝟐\mathbf{K^{2}} in this basis by

𝒆λ′,𝒌∗⋅𝐊𝟐⋅𝒆λ,𝒌\displaystyle\boldsymbol{e}_{\lambda^{\prime},\boldsymbol{k}}^{*}\cdot\mathbf{K^{2}}\cdot\boldsymbol{e}_{\lambda,\boldsymbol{k}} ≡Kλ′​λ2.\displaystyle\equiv K^{2}_{\lambda^{\prime}\lambda}\,. (58)

We introduce phonon creation and annihilation operators b^λ,𝒌†\hat{b}^{\dagger}_{\lambda,\boldsymbol{k}}, b^λ,𝒌\hat{b}_{\lambda,\boldsymbol{k}} satisfying the usual (discretized) commutation relations, [b^λ,𝒌,b^λ′,𝒌′†]=δλ,λ′​δ𝒌,𝒌′[\hat{b}_{\lambda,\boldsymbol{k}},\,\hat{b}^{\dagger}_{\lambda^{\prime},\boldsymbol{k}^{\prime}}]=\delta_{\lambda,\lambda^{\prime}}\delta_{\boldsymbol{k},\boldsymbol{k}^{\prime}}, etc., based on the diagonal piece of the Hamiltonian:

𝑨~​(𝒌)\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\tilde{A}}(\boldsymbol{k}) =\displaystyle= N​Ω​∑λ12​ελ1/2​Kλ​λ​(b^λ,𝒌+b^λ,−𝒌†)​𝒆λ,𝒌,\displaystyle\sqrt{N\Omega}\sum_{\lambda}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\,\varepsilon_{\lambda}^{1/2}K_{\lambda\lambda}}}\,\bigl(\hat{b}_{\lambda,\boldsymbol{k}}+\hat{b}^{\dagger}_{\lambda,-\boldsymbol{k}}\bigr)\,\boldsymbol{e}_{\lambda,\boldsymbol{k}}\,, (59)
𝑷~​(𝒌)\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\tilde{P}}(\boldsymbol{k}) =\displaystyle= N​Ω​∑λελ1/2​Kλ​λ2​1i​(b^λ,𝒌−b^λ,−𝒌†)​𝒆λ,𝒌.\displaystyle\sqrt{N\Omega}\sum_{\lambda}\sqrt{\frac{\varepsilon_{\lambda}^{1/2}K_{\lambda\lambda}}{2}}\,\frac{1}{i}\bigl(\hat{b}_{\lambda,\boldsymbol{k}}-\hat{b}^{\dagger}_{\lambda,-\boldsymbol{k}}\bigr)\,\boldsymbol{e}_{\lambda,\boldsymbol{k}}\,. (60)

The photon Hamiltonian then becomes

HEM=∑𝒌[∑λ=12Kλ​λελ​b^λ,𝒌†​b^λ,𝒌+K1222​ε1​ε2​K11​K22​(b^1,−𝒌+b^1,𝒌†)​(b^2,𝒌+b^2,−𝒌†)],H_{\text{EM}}=\sum_{\boldsymbol{k}}\biggl[\sum_{\lambda=1}^{2}\frac{K_{\lambda\lambda}}{\sqrt{\varepsilon_{\lambda}}}\,\hat{b}_{\lambda,\boldsymbol{k}}^{\dagger}\hat{b}_{\lambda,\boldsymbol{k}}\,+\frac{K_{12}^{2}}{2\sqrt{\sqrt{\varepsilon_{1}\varepsilon_{2}}K_{11}K_{22}}}\bigl(\hat{b}_{1,-\boldsymbol{k}}+\hat{b}^{\dagger}_{1,\boldsymbol{k}}\bigr)\bigl(\hat{b}_{2,\boldsymbol{k}}+\hat{b}^{\dagger}_{2,-\boldsymbol{k}}\bigr)\biggr]\,, (61)

where we have used K12=K21K_{12}=K_{21}.

Finally, the photon-phonon mixing term HmixH_{\text{mix}} can be written in terms of the creation and annihilation operators according to Eqs. (12) and (59):

Hmix\displaystyle H_{\text{mix}} =\displaystyle= −eN​Ω∑𝒌∑l​jei​𝒌⋅𝒙l​j0mj𝑨~(𝒌)⋅𝐙j∗⋅𝒑l​j\displaystyle-\frac{e}{N\Omega}\sum_{\boldsymbol{k}}\sum_{lj}\frac{e^{i\boldsymbol{k}\cdot\boldsymbol{x}_{lj}^{0}}}{m_{j}}\boldsymbol{\tilde{A}}(\boldsymbol{k})\cdot\mathbf{Z}^{*}_{j}\cdot\boldsymbol{p}_{lj} (62)
=\displaystyle= i​e2​Ω​∑𝒌∑ν=13​n∑λ=12ων,𝒌ελ1/2​Kλ​λ​(𝒆λ,−𝒌⋅𝝃ν,𝒌)​(a^ν,𝒌−a^ν,−𝒌†)​(b^λ,−𝒌+b^λ,𝒌†).\displaystyle\frac{ie}{2\sqrt{\Omega}}\sum_{\boldsymbol{k}}\sum_{\nu=1}^{3n}\sum_{\lambda=1}^{2}\sqrt{\frac{\omega_{\nu,\boldsymbol{k}}}{\varepsilon_{\lambda}^{1/2}K_{\lambda\lambda}}}\,\bigl(\boldsymbol{e}_{\lambda,-\boldsymbol{k}}\cdot\boldsymbol{\xi}_{\nu,\boldsymbol{k}}\bigr)\bigl(\hat{a}_{\nu,\boldsymbol{k}}-\hat{a}^{\dagger}_{\nu,-\boldsymbol{k}}\bigr)\bigl(\hat{b}_{\lambda,-\boldsymbol{k}}+\hat{b}^{\dagger}_{\lambda,\boldsymbol{k}}\bigr)\,.

The total quadratic Hamiltonian, given by the sum of Eqs. (51), Eqs. (54), Eqs. (61) and Eqs. (62), involves the 3​n3n phonon and 2 photon creation/annihilation operators, a^ν=(1,…,3​n),𝒌(†)\hat{a}^{(\dagger)}_{\nu=(1,\dots,3n),\boldsymbol{k}}, b^λ=(1,2),𝒌(†)\hat{b}^{(\dagger)}_{\lambda=(1,2),\boldsymbol{k}}. For simplicity, let us write a^ν=(3​n+1,3​n+2),𝒌(†)≡b^λ=(1,2),𝒌(†)\hat{a}^{(\dagger)}_{\nu=(3n+1,3n+2),\boldsymbol{k}}\equiv\hat{b}^{(\dagger)}_{\lambda=(1,2),\boldsymbol{k}}. The quadratic Hamiltonian then has the form:

H^=∑𝒌∈1​B​Z𝕒𝒌†⋅𝕙𝒌⋅𝕒𝒌with𝕒𝒌=[a^1,𝒌,…,a^3​n+2,𝒌,a^1,−𝒌†,…,a^3​n+2,−𝒌†]𝖳.\displaystyle\hat{H}=\sum_{\boldsymbol{k}\in 1{\textrm{B}Z}}\mathbb{a}^{\dagger}_{\boldsymbol{k}}\cdot\mathbb{h}_{\boldsymbol{k}}\cdot\mathbb{a}_{\boldsymbol{k}}\qquad\textrm{with}\qquad\mathbb{a}_{\boldsymbol{k}}=\left[\hat{a}_{1,\boldsymbol{k}},\ldots,\,\hat{a}_{3n+2,\boldsymbol{k}},\hat{a}^{\dagger}_{1,\boldsymbol{-k}},\ldots,\,\hat{a}^{\dagger}_{3n+2,\boldsymbol{-k}}\right]^{\mathsf{T}}\,. (63)

The matrix 𝕙𝒌\mathbb{h}_{\boldsymbol{k}} can be written as:

𝕙𝒌=( 𝔸𝒌𝔹𝒌∗​ 𝔸𝒌𝔹𝒌† 𝔹𝒌𝖳ℂ𝒌​ −𝔹𝒌𝖳ℂ𝒌  𝔸𝒌𝔹−𝒌​ 𝔸𝒌𝔹−𝒌 𝔹𝒌𝖳ℂ𝒌​ −𝔹𝒌𝖳ℂ𝒌),\displaystyle\mathbb{h}_{\boldsymbol{k}}=\left(\begin{array}[]{ccccc?ccccc}&&&\hskip-3.0pt\vline&\hfil\lx@intercol\vrule width=1.0&&&&\hskip-3.0pt\vline&\\ &\mathbb{A}_{\boldsymbol{k}}&&\hskip-3.0pt\vline&\mathbb{B}^{*}_{\boldsymbol{k}}\hfil\lx@intercol\vrule width=1.0&&\mathbb{A}_{\boldsymbol{k}}&&\hskip-3.0pt\vline&\mathbb{B}^{\dagger}_{\boldsymbol{k}}\\ &&&\hskip-3.0pt\vline&\hfil\lx@intercol\vrule width=1.0&&&&\hskip-3.0pt\vline&\\ \hline\cr&\mathbb{B}^{\mathsf{T}}_{\boldsymbol{k}}&&\hskip-3.0pt\vline&\mathbb{C}_{\boldsymbol{k}}\hfil\lx@intercol\vrule width=1.0&&-\mathbb{B}^{\mathsf{T}}_{\boldsymbol{k}}&&\hskip-3.0pt\vline&\mathbb{C}_{\boldsymbol{k}}\\ \cr\hrule height=1.0pt&&&\hskip-3.0pt\vline&\hfil\lx@intercol\vrule width=1.0&&&&\hskip-3.0pt\vline&\\ &\mathbb{A}_{\boldsymbol{k}}&&\hskip-3.0pt\vline&\mathbb{B}_{-\boldsymbol{k}}\hfil\lx@intercol\vrule width=1.0&&\mathbb{A}_{\boldsymbol{k}}&&\hskip-3.0pt\vline&\mathbb{B}_{-\boldsymbol{k}}\\ &&&\hskip-3.0pt\vline&\hfil\lx@intercol\vrule width=1.0&&&&\hskip-3.0pt\vline&\\ \hline\cr&\mathbb{B}^{\mathsf{T}}_{\boldsymbol{k}}&&\hskip-3.0pt\vline&\mathbb{C}_{\boldsymbol{k}}\hfil\lx@intercol\vrule width=1.0&&-\mathbb{B}^{\mathsf{T}}_{\boldsymbol{k}}&&\hskip-3.0pt\vline&\mathbb{C}_{\boldsymbol{k}}\end{array}\right),

where 𝔸𝒌\mathbb{A}_{\boldsymbol{k}} is a 3​n×3​n3n\times 3n matrix given by:

𝔸𝒌,ν​ν′=12​ων​δν​ν′+e24​Ω​ων,𝐤​ων′,𝐤​(𝐤⋅𝝃ν,𝐤∗)​(𝐤⋅𝝃ν′,𝐤)𝒌⋅𝜺⋅𝒌,\displaystyle\mathbb{A}_{\boldsymbol{k},\nu\nu^{\prime}}=\frac{1}{2}\omega_{\nu}\delta_{\nu\nu^{\prime}}+\frac{e^{2}}{4\Omega\sqrt{\omega_{\nu,\mathbf{k}}\omega_{\nu^{\prime},\mathbf{k}}}}\frac{(\mathbf{k}\cdot\boldsymbol{\xi}_{\nu,\mathbf{k}}^{*})(\mathbf{k}\cdot\boldsymbol{\xi}_{\nu^{\prime},\mathbf{k}})}{\boldsymbol{k}\cdot\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}\cdot\boldsymbol{k}}\,, (73)

while 𝔹𝒌\mathbb{B}_{\boldsymbol{k}} is a 3​n×23n\times 2 with the following structure

𝔹𝒌,ν​ν′=−∑λ=12i​e4​Ωων,𝐤εν′1/2​Kν′​ν′(𝝃ν,𝒌⋅𝒆ν′,−𝒌),\displaystyle\mathbb{B}_{\boldsymbol{k},\nu\nu^{\prime}}=-\sum_{\lambda=1}^{2}\frac{ie}{4\sqrt{\Omega}}\sqrt{\frac{\omega_{\nu,\mathbf{k}}}{\varepsilon_{\nu^{\prime}}^{1/2}K_{\nu^{\prime}\nu^{\prime}}}}\left(\boldsymbol{\xi}_{\nu,\boldsymbol{k}}\cdot\boldsymbol{e}_{\nu^{\prime},-\boldsymbol{k}}\right)\,, (74)

and ℂ𝒌,ν​ν′\mathbb{C}_{\boldsymbol{k},\nu\nu^{\prime}} is a 2×22\times 2 matrix given by

ℂ𝒌,ν​ν′=Kν​ν′24​εν​εν′​Kν​ν​Kν′​ν′.\displaystyle\mathbb{C}_{\boldsymbol{k},\nu\nu^{\prime}}=\frac{K_{\nu\nu^{\prime}}^{2}}{4\sqrt{\sqrt{\varepsilon_{\nu}\varepsilon_{\nu^{\prime}}}K_{\nu\nu}K_{\nu^{\prime}\nu^{\prime}}}}\,. (75)

We review a general algorithm for diagonalizing such Hamiltonians in Appendix C.

Appendix B General form of the magnon Hamiltonian

In this appendix, by following Ref. [45], we review the procedure to derive the quadratic Hamiltonian describing small fluctuations around the ground state of the spin lattice described by Eq. (19).55 5 We adopt a different phase convention compared to Ref. [45], by using ei​𝒌⋅𝒙l​je^{i\boldsymbol{k}\cdot\boldsymbol{x}_{lj}} as oppose to ei​𝒌⋅𝒙le^{i\boldsymbol{k}\cdot\boldsymbol{x}_{l}}, in the Fourier transform Eq. (22). The results we review will apply to both commensurate and single-QQ incommensurate materials (such as Ba3​NbFe3​Si2​O14\text{Ba}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{3}}}\text{NbFe}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{3}}}\text{Si}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\text{O}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{14}}} discussed in Sec. III). We conclude the appendix giving the generalization of the rate in Eq. (27) for the case of incommensurate materials.

To include in our discussion the case of single-QQ incommensurate materials, we need to generalize Eq. (20) to

𝑺l​j=𝐑′​(𝒙l​j)⋅𝐑j⋅𝑺l​j′,\displaystyle\boldsymbol{S}_{lj}=\mathbf{R}^{\prime}(\boldsymbol{x}_{lj})\cdot\mathbf{R}_{j}\cdot\boldsymbol{S}_{lj}^{\prime}\,, (76)

where the additional rotation 𝑹′​(𝒙l​j)\boldsymbol{R}^{\prime}(\boldsymbol{x}_{lj}) brings to a reference frame where the spin orientation looks the same in all the unit cells (for commensurate ordered materials, 𝑹′=𝟏\boldsymbol{R}^{\prime}=\mathbf{1}). Following the Holstein-Primakoff transformation, Eq. (21), we we can rewrite Eq. (76) as, at leading order,

𝑺l​j=𝐑′​(𝒙l​j)​[Sj2​(𝒓j∗​a^l​j+𝒓j​a^l​j†)+𝒕j​(Sj−a^l​j†​a^l​j)],\displaystyle\boldsymbol{S}_{lj}=\mathbf{R}^{\prime}(\boldsymbol{x}_{lj})\left[\sqrt{\frac{S_{j}}{2}}\left(\boldsymbol{r}^{*}_{j}\hat{a}_{lj}+\boldsymbol{r}_{j}\hat{a}_{lj}^{\dagger}\right)+\boldsymbol{t}_{j}\left(S_{j}-\hat{a}^{\dagger}_{lj}\hat{a}_{lj}\right)\right], (77)

where 𝒕j\boldsymbol{t}_{j} is a unit vector pointing along the direction of the jj-th spin in the rotating frame (i.e. the reference frame defined by the rotation 𝐑′\mathbf{R}^{\prime}), while 𝒓j\boldsymbol{r}_{j} and 𝒓j∗\boldsymbol{r}_{j}^{*} span an orthogonal coordinate system. These vectors are related to the components of the matrix 𝐑j\mathbf{R}_{j} by

𝒓jα=𝐑jα​1+i​𝐑jα​2𝒕jα=𝐑jα​3.\displaystyle\boldsymbol{r}_{j}^{\alpha}=\mathbf{R}_{j}^{\alpha 1}+i\mathbf{R}_{j}^{\alpha 2}\qquad\qquad\boldsymbol{t}_{j}^{\alpha}=\mathbf{R}_{j}^{\alpha 3}\,. (78)

By substituting Eq. (77) into Eq. (19), and going to momentum space, we obtain the following expression for the quadratic part of the Hamiltonian

H^=∑𝒌∈1​B​Z𝕒𝒌†⋅𝕙𝒌⋅𝕒𝒌with𝕒𝒌=[a^1,𝒌,…,a^n,𝒌,a^1,−𝒌†,…,a^n,−𝒌†]𝖳.\displaystyle\hat{H}=\sum_{\boldsymbol{k}\in 1{\textrm{B}Z}}\mathbb{a}^{\dagger}_{\boldsymbol{k}}\cdot\mathbb{h}_{\boldsymbol{k}}\cdot\mathbb{a}_{\boldsymbol{k}}\qquad\textrm{with}\qquad\mathbb{a}_{\boldsymbol{k}}=\left[\hat{a}_{1,\boldsymbol{k}},\ldots,\,\hat{a}_{n,\boldsymbol{k}},\hat{a}^{\dagger}_{1,\boldsymbol{-k}},\ldots,\,\hat{a}^{\dagger}_{n,\boldsymbol{-k}}\right]^{\mathsf{T}}\,. (79)

The matrix 𝕙𝒌\mathbb{h}_{\boldsymbol{k}} can be written in terms of n×nn\times n sub-matrices as:

𝕙𝒌=(𝔸𝒌−ℂ𝔹𝒌𝔹𝒌†𝔸−𝒌∗−ℂ)\displaystyle\mathbb{h}_{\boldsymbol{k}}=\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}\mathbb{A}_{\boldsymbol{k}}-\mathbb{C}&\mathbb{B}_{\boldsymbol{k}}\\ \mathbb{B}^{\dagger}_{\boldsymbol{k}}&\mathbb{A}^{*}_{-\boldsymbol{k}}-\mathbb{C}\end{array}\right)

where, by defining 𝐉l​j,l′​j′′=𝐑′​(𝒙l​j)𝖳⋅𝐉l​j,l′​j′⋅𝐑′​(𝒙l′​j′)\mathbf{J}^{\prime}_{lj,l^{\prime}j^{\prime}}=\mathbf{R}^{\prime}(\boldsymbol{x}_{lj})^{\mathsf{T}}\cdot\mathbf{J}_{lj,l^{\prime}j^{\prime}}\cdot\mathbf{R}^{\prime}(\boldsymbol{x}_{l^{\prime}j^{\prime}}), we have

𝔸𝒌,j​j′=𝔸𝒌,j​j′†=Sj​Sj′2​𝒓j𝖳⋅𝐉−𝒌,j​j′′⋅𝒓j′∗−12​μB​δj​j′​𝑩𝖳⋅gj⋅𝒕j𝔹𝒌,j​j′=𝔹𝒌,j​j′∗=Sj​Sj′2​𝒓j𝖳⋅𝐉−𝒌,j​j′′⋅𝒓j′ℂ𝒌,j​j′=δj​j′​∑lSl​𝒕j𝖳⋅𝐉j​l′​(0)⋅𝒕l.\displaystyle\begin{aligned} \mathbb{A}_{\boldsymbol{k},jj^{\prime}}&=\mathbb{A}^{\dagger}_{\boldsymbol{k},jj^{\prime}}=\frac{\sqrt{S_{j}S_{j^{\prime}}}}{2}\boldsymbol{r}_{j}^{\mathsf{T}}\cdot\mathbf{J}^{\prime}_{-\boldsymbol{k},jj^{\prime}}\cdot\boldsymbol{r}_{j^{\prime}}^{*}-\frac{1}{2}\mu_{\textrm{B}}\delta_{jj^{\prime}}\,\boldsymbol{B}^{\mathsf{T}}\cdot g_{j}\cdot\boldsymbol{t}_{j}\\ \mathbb{B}_{\boldsymbol{k},jj^{\prime}}&=\mathbb{B}^{*}_{\boldsymbol{k},jj^{\prime}}=\frac{\sqrt{S_{j}S_{j^{\prime}}}}{2}\boldsymbol{r}_{j}^{\mathsf{T}}\cdot\mathbf{J}^{\prime}_{-\boldsymbol{k},jj^{\prime}}\cdot\boldsymbol{r}_{j^{\prime}}\\ \mathbb{C}_{\boldsymbol{k},jj^{\prime}}&=\delta_{jj^{\prime}}\sum_{l}S_{l}\,\boldsymbol{t}_{j}^{\mathsf{T}}\cdot\mathbf{J}^{\prime}_{jl}(0)\cdot\boldsymbol{t}_{l}\end{aligned}\,. (83)

The procedure to diagonalize Hamiltonian of this kind is reviewed in Appendix C.

We conclude by generalizing to the incommensurate case the formula for magnon production given in Eq. (27). We start by writing the rotation matrix 𝑹′​(𝒙l​j)\boldsymbol{R}^{\prime}(\boldsymbol{x}_{lj}) in terms of the propagation vector which characterizes the incommensurate order 𝑸=(τ1,τ2,τ3)\boldsymbol{Q}=(\tau_{1},\tau_{2},\tau_{3}):

𝐑′​(𝒙l​j)=ℛ⁡(𝒏|𝑸⋅𝒙l​j),\mathbf{R}^{\prime}(\boldsymbol{x}_{lj})=\mathcal{R}(\boldsymbol{n}\,|\,\boldsymbol{Q}\cdot\boldsymbol{x}_{lj})\,, (84)

where ℛ⁡(𝒏|φ)\mathcal{R}(\boldsymbol{n}\,|\,\varphi) is the rotation matrix around the unit vector 𝒏\boldsymbol{n} by an angle φ\varphi:

ℛ⁡(𝒏|φ)=Re​[ei​φ​(𝟏−i​𝐧×−𝒏​𝒏T)]+𝒏​𝒏T=𝐑0′+𝐑+′​ei​φ+𝐑−′​e−i​φ\displaystyle\mathcal{R}(\boldsymbol{n}\,|\,\varphi)=\text{Re}\bigl[e^{i\varphi}(\boldsymbol{1}-i\mathbf{n}_{\times}-\boldsymbol{n}\boldsymbol{n}^{T})\bigr]+\boldsymbol{n}\boldsymbol{n}^{T}=\mathbf{R}^{\prime}_{0}+\mathbf{R}^{\prime}_{+}e^{i\varphi}+\mathbf{R}^{\prime}_{-}e^{-i\varphi} (85)
𝐑0′=𝒏​𝒏T,𝐑±′=12​(𝟏∓i​𝐧×−𝒏​𝒏T),𝐧×=(0−nznynz0−nx−nynx0),\displaystyle\mathbf{R}^{\prime}_{0}=\boldsymbol{n}\boldsymbol{n}^{T}\,,\qquad\mathbf{R}^{\prime}_{\pm}=\frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{1}\mp i\mathbf{n}_{\times}-\boldsymbol{n}\boldsymbol{n}^{T})\,,\qquad\mathbf{n}_{\times}=\left(\begin{matrix}0&-n_{z}&n_{y}\\ n_{z}&0&-n_{x}\\ -n_{y}&n_{x}&0\end{matrix}\right)\,, (86)

noting that 𝐧×⋅𝒗=𝒏×𝒗\mathbf{n}_{\times}\cdot\boldsymbol{v}=\boldsymbol{n}\times\boldsymbol{v} for any vector 𝒗\boldsymbol{v}. Then, by using Eq. (76) and the interaction given by Eq. (4), we find

⟨ν,𝒌​|δ​H0^|​0⟩\displaystyle\langle\nu,\boldsymbol{k}|\hat{\delta H_{0}}|0\rangle =\displaystyle= ∑l​jSj2​Ne−i𝒌⋅𝒙l​j𝒇j⋅𝐑′(𝒙l​j)⋅(𝕍j​ν,−𝒌𝒓j∗+𝕌j​ν,𝒌∗𝒓j)\displaystyle\sum_{lj}\sqrt{\frac{S_{j}}{2N}}\,e^{-i\boldsymbol{k}\cdot\boldsymbol{x}_{lj}}\,\boldsymbol{f}_{j}\cdot\mathbf{R}^{\prime}(\boldsymbol{x}_{lj})\cdot\bigl(\mathbb{V}_{j\nu,-\boldsymbol{k}}\boldsymbol{r}_{j}^{*}+\mathbb{U}^{*}_{j\nu,\boldsymbol{k}}\boldsymbol{r}_{j}\bigr) (87)
=\displaystyle= N2​∑jSj​𝒇j⋅(δ𝒌,𝟎​𝐑0′+δ𝒌,𝑸​𝐑+′+δ𝒌,−𝑸​𝐑−′)⋅(𝕍j​ν,−𝒌​𝒓j∗+𝕌j​ν,𝒌∗​𝒓j),\displaystyle\sqrt{\frac{N}{2}}\sum_{j}\sqrt{S_{j}}\,\boldsymbol{f}_{j}\cdot\bigl(\delta_{\boldsymbol{k},\boldsymbol{0}}\mathbf{R}^{\prime}_{0}+\delta_{\boldsymbol{k},\boldsymbol{Q}}\,\mathbf{R}^{\prime}_{+}+\delta_{\boldsymbol{k},-\boldsymbol{Q}}\,\mathbf{R}^{\prime}_{-}\bigr)\cdot\bigl(\mathbb{V}_{j\nu,-\boldsymbol{k}}\boldsymbol{r}_{j}^{*}+\mathbb{U}^{*}_{j\nu,\boldsymbol{k}}\boldsymbol{r}_{j}\bigr)\,,

from which we can obtain the generalized expression for the rate:

R𝑸≠0=2​ωmcell​∑ν=1n∑λ=−11ων,λ​𝑸​γν,λ​𝑸(ω2−ων,λ​𝑸2)2+(ω​γν,λ​𝑸)2​|∑jSj​𝒇jT​𝐑λ′​(𝕍j​ν,−λ​𝑸​𝒓j∗+𝕌j​ν,λ​𝑸∗​𝒓j)|2.R_{\boldsymbol{Q}\neq 0}=\frac{2\omega}{m_{\text{cell}}}\sum_{\nu=1}^{n}\sum_{\lambda=-1}^{1}\,\frac{\omega_{\nu,\lambda\boldsymbol{Q}}\,\gamma_{\nu,\lambda\boldsymbol{Q}}}{(\omega^{2}-\omega_{\nu,\lambda\boldsymbol{Q}}^{2})^{2}+(\omega\,\gamma_{\nu,\lambda\boldsymbol{Q}})^{2}}\,\biggl|\sum_{j}\sqrt{S_{j}}\,\boldsymbol{f}_{j}^{T}\,\mathbf{R}^{\prime}_{\lambda}\,\bigl(\mathbb{V}_{j\nu,-\lambda\boldsymbol{Q}}\boldsymbol{r}_{j}^{*}+\mathbb{U}^{*}_{j\nu,\lambda\boldsymbol{Q}}\boldsymbol{r}_{j}\bigr)\biggr|^{2}\,. (88)

Appendix C Diagonalization of quadratic Hamiltonians

In this appendix, by closely following Ref. [45, 46], we review the procedure to diagonalize quadratic Hamiltonians which have the form of Eq. (63) and Eq. (79). The goal of the procedure is to find a homogeneous linear transformation

𝕒𝒌=𝕋𝒌⋅𝕒𝒌′≡𝕋𝒌⋅[a^1,𝒌′,…,a^n,𝒌′,a^1,−𝒌′⁣†,…,a^n,−𝒌′⁣†]𝖳,\displaystyle\mathbb{a}_{\boldsymbol{k}}=\mathbb{T}_{\boldsymbol{k}}\cdot\mathbb{a}_{\boldsymbol{k}}^{\prime}\equiv\mathbb{T}_{\boldsymbol{k}}\cdot\left[\hat{a}_{1,\boldsymbol{k}}^{\prime},\ldots,\,\hat{a}_{n,\boldsymbol{k}}^{\prime},\hat{a}^{\prime\dagger}_{1,-\boldsymbol{k}},\ldots,\,\hat{a}^{\prime\dagger}_{n,-\boldsymbol{k}}\right]^{\mathsf{T}}\,, (89)

such that the operators a^ν,𝒌′\hat{a}^{\prime}_{\nu,\boldsymbol{k}}, a^ν,𝒌′†\hat{a}_{\nu,\boldsymbol{k}}^{{}^{\prime}\dagger} satisfy the canonical commutation relations

[𝕒𝒌′,𝕒𝒌′⁣†]=(𝟙00−𝟙)≡𝕘,\displaystyle[\mathbb{a}_{\boldsymbol{k}}^{\prime},\mathbb{a}_{\boldsymbol{k}}^{\prime\dagger}]=\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}\mathbb{1}&0\\ 0&-\mathbb{1}\end{array}\right)\equiv\mathbb{g}\,,

and that rewrites the quadratic Hamiltonian as

H^\displaystyle\hat{H} =∑𝒌𝕒𝒌†​𝕙𝒌​𝕒𝒌=∑𝒌𝕒𝒌′⁣†⋅𝔼⋅𝕒𝒌′,\displaystyle=\sum_{\boldsymbol{k}}\mathbb{a}^{\dagger}_{\boldsymbol{k}}\mathbb{h}_{\boldsymbol{k}}\mathbb{a}_{\boldsymbol{k}}=\sum_{\boldsymbol{k}}\mathbb{a}^{\prime\dagger}_{\boldsymbol{k}}\cdot\mathbb{E}\cdot\mathbb{a}^{\prime}_{\boldsymbol{k}}\,, (93)

where

𝔼𝒌≡𝕋𝒌†⋅𝕙𝒌⋅𝕋𝒌=12​diag​(ω1,𝒌​…​ωn,𝒌,ω1,𝒌​…​ωn,𝒌)withων,𝒌>0.\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\boldsymbol{k}}\equiv\mathbb{T}^{\dagger}_{\boldsymbol{k}}\cdot\mathbb{h}_{\boldsymbol{k}}\cdot\mathbb{T}_{\boldsymbol{k}}=\frac{1}{2}\,\textrm{diag}\left(\omega_{1,\boldsymbol{k}}\ldots\omega_{n,\boldsymbol{k}},\omega_{1,\boldsymbol{k}}\ldots\omega_{n,\boldsymbol{k}}\right)\qquad\textrm{with}\qquad\omega_{\nu,\boldsymbol{k}}>0\,. (94)

By using the commutation relations in Eq. (C), it can be easily shown that, up to constant terms, Eq. (93) is equivalent to Eq. (14) and Eq. (23) with the 𝕌\mathbb{U} and 𝕍\mathbb{V} matrices implicitly defined as

𝕋𝒌=(𝕌j​ν,𝒌𝕍j​ν,𝒌𝕍j​ν,−𝒌∗𝕌j​ν,−𝒌∗).\displaystyle\mathbb{T}_{\boldsymbol{k}}=\left(\begin{matrix}\mathbb{U}_{j\nu,\boldsymbol{k}}&\mathbb{V}_{j\nu,\boldsymbol{k}}\\ \mathbb{V}_{j\nu,-\boldsymbol{k}}^{*}&\mathbb{U}_{j\nu,-\boldsymbol{k}}^{*}\end{matrix}\right)\,. (95)

Such diagonalization procedure (usually called para-unitary diagonalization) can be achieved if 𝕙⁡(𝒌)\mathbb{h}(\boldsymbol{k}) is positive definite. If the spectrum contains zero energy modes, the 𝕙⁡(𝒌)\mathbb{h}(\boldsymbol{k}) matrix will be positive semidefinite and such para-unitary diagonalization may not exist. This problem can be cured by adding a small ϵ\epsilon value to the diagonal components of 𝕙⁡(𝒌)\mathbb{h}(\boldsymbol{k}) [46]. This introduces a small and negligible shift in the spectrum but makes 𝕙⁡(𝒌)\mathbb{h}(\boldsymbol{k}) positive definite and allows for a para-unitary diagonalization. Ref. [46] provides a simple three-step algorithm to find the linear transformation 𝕋\mathbb{T} and the associated eigenvalues:

  • •

    A Cholesky decomposition is applied to find a complex matrix 𝕂𝒌\mathbb{K}_{\boldsymbol{k}} such that 𝕙𝒌=𝕂𝒌†​𝕂𝒌\mathbb{h}_{\boldsymbol{k}}=\mathbb{K}_{\boldsymbol{k}}^{\dagger}\mathbb{K}_{\boldsymbol{k}}.

  • •

    The eigenvalue problem for the Hermitian matrix 𝕂𝒌​𝕘𝕂𝒌†\mathbb{K}_{\boldsymbol{k}}\mathbb{g}\mathbb{K}_{\boldsymbol{k}}^{\dagger} is solved, and the resulting eigenvalues used to form the columns of the matrix 𝕌𝒌\mathbb{U}_{\boldsymbol{k}}. The order of the columns is chosen such that the first NN elements of the diagonalized matrix 𝕃=𝕌†​𝕂𝒌​𝕘𝕂𝒌†​𝕌\mathbb{L}=\mathbb{U}^{\dagger}\mathbb{K}_{\boldsymbol{k}}\mathbb{g}\mathbb{K}^{\dagger}_{\boldsymbol{k}}\mathbb{U} are positive and the last NN negative.

  • •

    Finally, the matrix 𝔼𝒌\mathbb{E}_{\boldsymbol{k}} in Eq. (94) is simply related to 𝕃𝒌\mathbb{L}_{\boldsymbol{k}} by 𝔼𝒌=𝕘𝕃𝒌\mathbb{E}_{\boldsymbol{k}}=\mathbb{g}\mathbb{L}_{\boldsymbol{k}}, and the 𝕋𝒌\mathbb{T}_{\boldsymbol{k}} matrix is given by 𝕋𝒌=𝕂𝒌−1​𝕌𝒌​𝔼𝒌1/2\mathbb{T}_{\boldsymbol{k}}=\mathbb{K}_{\boldsymbol{k}}^{-1}\mathbb{U}_{\boldsymbol{k}}\mathbb{E}_{\boldsymbol{k}}^{1/2}.
